oneLine: Bitcoin and Ethereum each rose under 1% on Tuesday, November 3 as US Congressional Elections took place at 15:16 UTC and the CFTC approved equity perpetual futures, with altcoins broadly bullish and top traders heavily long.
caveman: On Tuesday, November 3, two important things happened in the US: voters held Congressional midterm elections while crypto markets were open, and the government approved a new trading product called equity perpetual futures. Bitcoin went up 0.84% to $77,441 and Ethereum up 0.93% to $2,273—steady gains, not dramatic. About 7 out of 10 other cryptocurrencies also went up. The biggest traders bet heavily that prices would keep rising (about 2.6 traders betting UP for every 1 betting DOWN). One strange signal: Bitcoin funding was positive (longs paying shorts about 3% per year), meaning traders were confident Bitcoin would climb. But Ethereum's funding was negative, meaning shorts were confident even though the price went up. Asian computer-chip stocks fell a lot because a big company announced a huge AI spending plan, which made people worry about profit. It was a calm day—markets reacted to the election results but didn't panic.
priceVolumeSummary: Bitcoin closed at $77,441.70 and Ethereum at $2,273.85, with all five major venues within $13 and $2 of these prices respectively, showing strong consensus. Binance led trading volume on both assets: $8.46 billion on Bitcoin and $5.57 billion on Ethereum, followed by Bybit, OKX, Bitget, and Gate.
positioningSummary: Bitcoin's funding rate was positive at 3.16% annualized—a bullish signal that longs were willing to pay shorts for the privilege of staying long. Ethereum's funding was negative at −1.49%, suggesting shorts remained confident despite the price gain, creating a contrast between the two assets. Open interest rose modestly on Bitcoin (+0.48% in dollar terms) but more sharply on Ethereum (+2.63%), showing traders were adding leverage, especially on Ethereum. Long traders heavily outnumbered short traders across both: 2.6-to-1 on Bitcoin and 2.64-to-1 on Ethereum. The largest traders were even more bullish: 1.87-to-1 on Bitcoin and 1.60-to-1 on Ethereum. Buyers were slightly more aggressive than sellers (taker buy/sell ratio 1.02 on Bitcoin, 1.05 on Ethereum). Market breadth remained very strong with 70.4% of Binance altcoins advancing, showing the bullish sentiment was broad.
stocksSummary: Asian semiconductor stocks fell sharply on November 3: South Korea's SK Hynix dropped 7.58% and Samsung 5.63%, with their leveraged ETFs hit harder (SK Hynix 2x down 14.73%, Samsung 2x down 10.93%). The primary catalyst was Oracle's announcement of a $20 billion AI fundraising plan, which triggered concerns about AI profitability and whether heavy AI spending could translate to returns. Chinese tech was mixed—AI stocks like Unitree Robotics and CXMT gained 2.54% and 5.87%, while Tencent and Xiaomi edged up. The KOSPI (Seoul stock index) fell 5.3% as South Korean investors net-sold on the AI doubts.

movers.explanation: AGT fell 27.4% over the prior 24 hours but reversed sharply, closing the day up 32.9%, a strong recovery that suggests square-off buying or a short squeeze. No specific catalyst identified in public reporting.

HOT dropped 19.1% in the prior 24 hours but rebounded 26.0% on the day, showing a similar reversal pattern to AGTUSDT. The rebound suggests algorithmic buying or liquidation cascade rather than news-driven movement.

BMT gained 10.4% over the prior 24 hours and continued upward with a 23.6% daily gain, showing sustained upward momentum. The consistency suggests continued buyer support or event-driven accumulation.

topThree.headline: US Congressional Elections — Democrats win control of Congress
topThree.what: US voters held Congressional midterm elections on November 3 at 15:16 UTC during the US market session. Early results indicated a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress. Markets initially reacted with caution—Bitcoin dipped below $76,000 as uncertainty peaked—but recovered above $78,000 by November 4 as traders absorbed the outcome. The political shift raises expectations for stricter crypto regulation under a Democratic-controlled SEC and CFTC, though removes near-term policy whiplash.

topThree.headline: CFTC Approves Equity Perpetual Futures — new US stock derivatives market launches
topThree.what: The US CFTC approved equity perpetual futures under Regulation 40.3, allowing regulated platforms to offer Bitcoin-settled perpetual contracts on individual US stocks. Trading became effective November 3, 2026. Kalshi Inc. launched equity perps contracts the same day. This expands crypto exchanges' product range into equities derivatives and represents the second major perpetual-futures approval by the CFTC in 2026 (Bitcoin perps were approved earlier in the year).

topThree.headline: Oracle Announces $20B AI Fundraising — triggers Asian semiconductor sell-off
topThree.what: Oracle announced a $20 billion AI infrastructure fundraising plan on November 3, immediately sparking concerns among investors about AI profitability and oversaturation of AI spending. South Korean semiconductor stocks (SK Hynix, Samsung) fell sharply, with the KOSPI index down 5.3% as foreign investors net-sold. The move highlights ongoing skepticism about whether massive AI infrastructure outlays can generate competitive returns.
topThree.coins: Tech perps (HKEX/KRX equities affected), downstream to crypto sentiment

Regulation and policy.headline: US Congressional Elections shift political landscape — crypto faces tighter oversight
Regulation and policy.what: Democratic victories in US Congressional midterms on November 3 will shift control of both chambers, changing crypto policy outlook. Industry observers noted the 'Clarity Act'—a bipartisan bill favored by the crypto industry—is unlikely to pass, and the SEC and CFTC will face Democratic-majority oversight, raising expectations for stricter rules on stablecoins, market structure, and exchange custody practices.

Institutional flows and ETFs.headline: BTC and ETH ETF flows show mixed sentiment around elections
Institutional flows and ETFs.what: Bitcoin ETFs recorded a net outflow of $115.6 million on November 3 as election results came in, with IBIT accounting for $95 million of the outflow. Ethereum ETFs were heavier sellers with $85.3 million net outflow. On November 4, sentiment reversed: Bitcoin ETFs rebounded with $74.6 million net inflow (FBTC +$236.7M, offset by IBIT -$201.2M), and Ethereum saw $53 million inflow. The outflows on election day reflect risk-off positioning ahead of the results; the November 4 rebound suggests buyer relief after the Democratic sweep was absorbed.

Exchange and platform changes.headline: CFTC Green-Lights Equity Perpetual Futures — Bitcoin-settled stock derivatives now live
Exchange and platform changes.what: The CFTC approved equity perpetual futures under Regulation 40.3 effective November 3, 2026. These new contracts allow regulated crypto exchanges and platforms to offer perpetual derivatives on individual US stocks, settled in Bitcoin. Kalshi Inc. and other venues immediately launched trading. The products are classified as security futures under the Commodity Futures Modernization Act of 2000 and face joint CFTC/SEC oversight.

Traditional markets.headline: Oracle $20B AI Spending Announcement Crashes Asian Semiconductors
Traditional markets.what: Oracle announced a $20 billion AI infrastructure fundraising commitment on November 3, immediately triggering a broad reassessment of AI profitability among investors. South Korean semiconductor stocks—SK Hynix (down 7.58%) and Samsung Electronics (down 5.63%)—fell sharply as foreign investors net-sold on concerns that massive AI capex cannot justify returns. The KOSPI index (Seoul) closed down 5.3%, with approximately $144 billion in market cap erased from Samsung and SK Hynix alone.
Traditional markets.coins: No direct crypto exposure; affects crypto sentiment via risk assets
Traditional markets.source: SBS News, Invezz, Seoul Economic Daily

etfFlows.summary: Bitcoin spot ETFs: $115.6M net outflow on Nov 3 (IBIT -$95M), then $74.6M net inflow on Nov 4 (FBTC +$236.7M, IBIT -$201.2M). Ethereum spot ETFs: $85.3M net outflow on Nov 3, $53M net inflow on Nov 4. Nov 3 outflows reflect pre-election caution; Nov 4 inflows suggest relief buying after Democratic sweep.

calendarNotes.typicalReaction: Crypto markets typically react sharply to political shifts affecting regulatory outlook. Democratic control of Congress raises expectations for stricter SEC/CFTC oversight of stablecoins and market structure—a medium-term headwind. However, regulatory clarity (once enacted) often reduces long-term uncertainty and can stabilize markets.

calendarNotes.event: CFTC Approves Equity Perpetual Futures (Nov 3, effective immediately)
calendarNotes.typicalReaction: Expansion of Bitcoin-settled products typically supports sentiment by deepening crypto's institutional role and use cases. Equity perps on crypto venues may drive incremental Bitcoin settlement demand.

calendarNotes.event: Norges Bank Rate Decision (Nov 5, 09:00 UTC) and Bank of England MPC Rate Decision (Nov 5, 12:00 UTC)
calendarNotes.typicalReaction: Central bank rate decisions often trigger volatility in risk assets including crypto. Hawkish surprises tend to weaken crypto; dovish surprises strengthen it relative to equities.

Employment data is a major US economic release and often triggers crypto volatility due to inflation and monetary policy implications. Strong jobs growth can be risk-on (bullish); weak growth is risk-off (bearish).

glossary.definition: The amount (as a percentage per year) that traders holding long positions pay to those holding short positions, or vice versa. Positive funding means longs pay shorts—a bullish signal that leverage is favoring higher prices. Negative funding means shorts pay longs—bearish. Rates are quoted as 8-hour intervals, annualized for comparison across venues.
A long trader bets that the price will rise. A short trader bets that the price will fall. The ratio of long to short positions shows the balance of bullish vs. bearish traders.

The proportion of traders holding long positions compared to those holding short positions (e.g., 2.6-to-1 means 2.6 long traders for every 1 short trader). A higher ratio indicates more bullish positioning; a lower ratio more bearish.

The settlement price used on a futures contract, typically a weighted average of the futures price and the spot price. Used to prevent manipulation and ensure contracts stay close to true market value.

The total number of active long or short contracts that have not yet been closed. An increase in open interest means traders are adding to their positions (bullish if price rises, suggesting conviction); a decrease means traders are reducing exposure.

The percentage increase or decrease in open interest over the report period, shown in dollar terms or in coin quantity. Rising open interest during an uptrend suggests strong momentum; falling suggests weakening conviction.

The proportion of aggressive buying (taker buy) to aggressive selling (taker sell) on a contract. A ratio above 1.0 indicates more aggressive buying than selling; below 1.0 indicates more selling pressure.

The long-to-short ratio among the largest traders on an exchange (typically the top 10–50 accounts by position size). This shows whether the biggest players are bullish or bearish; often more predictive than the broader trader population.

The percentage of assets in a market that gained value on the report day. High breadth (e.g., 70% of coins up) signals broad market strength; low breadth suggests weakness is concentrated in a few assets while most others are struggling.

A crypto derivative that mimics a spot price but never expires, unlike traditional futures. Traders pay each other funding rates to stay long or short indefinitely. Bitcoin-settled equity perpetuals allow trading stocks via Bitcoin-denominated contracts on crypto platforms.
A cryptocurrency platform where traders buy, sell, or trade futures contracts. This report covers Binance, Bybit, OKX, Bitget, and Gate—the five largest venues for crypto derivatives globally.
The total notional US-dollar amount traded in a contract over the report day.

The net change in assets under management for an exchange-traded fund. An outflow means investors net-redeemed shares (selling), suggesting bearish sentiment. An inflow means investors net-bought shares, suggesting bullish sentiment.
